unit.name: Pride and Prejudice
unit.subtitle: 19th Century: love, class and social expectations

lessons.title: Context: Regency Society
lessons.description: Austen’s Regency world, the marriage market, and why money defines everything in the novel.
lessons.content_html:
Jane Austen — Life and Influences

Jane Austen (1775–1817) published Pride and Prejudice in 1813. She was the daughter of a country clergyman and lived within the landed gentry — the class she writes about with precision and irony. Austen never married, and her novels explore the limited choices available to women with sharp social commentary.

For the OCR J352 exam, context (AO3) must be embedded within analysis. Austen’s world is one of strict hierarchy, where a woman’s future depended almost entirely on the man she married. Every conversation about money in the novel is a matter of survival, not mere romance.

Key Fact

The Bennet estate is entailed to Mr Collins, meaning the five Bennet sisters will have no home when their father dies. Mrs Bennet’s desperation to marry her daughters off is economic survival, not mere social ambition.

The Marriage Market

The famous opening — “It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife” — is deeply ironic. The “truth” is actually the assumption of mothers like Mrs Bennet. Austen immediately signals her novel will examine the gap between what society claims and what motivates people.

Austen presents four models of marriage: Charlotte/Collins (pragmatic), Lydia/Wickham (reckless), Jane/Bingley (gentle affection), Elizabeth/Darcy (intellectual equality). Each reflects a different response to Regency pressures.

Within the gentry, sharp distinctions existed. Darcy (£10,000/year, Pemberley) is near the top. The Bennets (modest income, no sons) are near the bottom. Bingley’s wealth comes from trade, making his family socially inferior despite their wealth. Caroline Bingley looks down on the Bennets; Lady Catherine considers Elizabeth beneath Darcy.

Regency women could not own property, enter professions or vote. Charlotte Lucas’s decision to marry Collins is entirely rational: “I am not romantic, you know; I never was. I ask only a comfortable home.” Austen asks whether Elizabeth’s idealism is a luxury only a younger, prettier woman can afford.

Key Fact

Four marriages explore the range of choices: Charlotte/Collins = survival, Lydia/Wickham = recklessness, Jane/Bingley = affection, Elizabeth/Darcy = intellectual equality achieved through overcoming pride and prejudice.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about context, always connect it to a specific text moment. Instead of “Women had limited options,” write: “Charlotte’s acceptance of Collins reflects the economic reality that Regency women without independent wealth had to choose between loveless marriage and dependency.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Austen uses irony to expose the gap between social ideals and economic realities in Regency England.
  • Marriage was the primary route to financial security for women — the entail makes Mrs Bennet’s urgency a survival matter.
  • The four marriages represent different responses to class, money and social expectation.

lessons.title: The Assembly & First Impressions
lessons.description: The Bennet family, Darcy’s pride at Meryton, and how first impressions shape the plot.
lessons.content_html:
The Bennet Family

The novel opens by introducing the Bennet family of Longbourn: five daughters, a sardonic father and an anxious mother. Mr Bennet retreats into his library and his irony; Mrs Bennet schemes to marry her daughters to wealthy men. Austen uses their contrasting reactions to the arrival of Mr Bingley at Netherfield Park to establish the novel’s comic tone and the tension between romantic idealism and economic pragmatism that runs through every chapter.

The five sisters represent a spectrum of Regency womanhood: Jane is gentle and trusting, Elizabeth is witty and independent, Mary is pedantic, Kitty is easily led, and Lydia is reckless. Austen positions Elizabeth as the heroine not because she is perfect, but because she combines intelligence with moral seriousness — qualities the other sisters lack in different ways.

Key Fact

Darcy dismisses Elizabeth as “tolerable, but not handsome enough to tempt me.” This public insult reveals his class pride — he considers the Bennets beneath his notice. Elizabeth’s response (“I could easily forgive his pride, if he had not mortified mine”) shows her prejudice forming: she judges Darcy on this single remark for much of the novel.

The Meryton Ball — First Impressions

The Meryton ball functions as a microcosm of Regency social dynamics. Dancing is a public performance of courtship: Bingley dances with Jane twice, signalling serious interest, while Darcy refuses to dance with anyone outside his party. To refuse a dance is a social insult — it signals that someone is beneath your notice. Darcy’s behaviour immediately establishes his pride as a social barrier.

Meanwhile, Mrs Bennet loudly boasts about Jane’s prospects, Lydia and Kitty flirt with officers, and Mary performs an embarrassing piano piece. The Bennet family’s social embarrassments undermine Jane and Elizabeth’s chances. Austen shows that in Regency England, you were judged not just by your own behaviour but by your family’s — a reality that will become critical when Lydia elopes.

The word “tolerable” is carefully chosen. It reduces Elizabeth from a person to an object to be assessed — she is not intolerable, merely not worth the effort. The conditional “not handsome enough to tempt me” implies Darcy sees himself as the prize, not the suitor. Austen uses this moment to establish the central irony: the man who seems most unpleasant will prove most worthy, and the woman he dismisses will become the one person who challenges him to grow.

Darcy and Elizabeth’s Early Dynamic

The contrast between Darcy and Bingley mirrors the contrast between Elizabeth and Jane. Bingley is open and generous; Darcy is reserved and judgmental. Jane sees the best in everyone; Elizabeth is perceptive but quick to condemn. Austen positions the reader to share Elizabeth’s amusement at Darcy’s expense, but later events will reveal that both Elizabeth and the reader have been as prejudiced as Darcy has been proud.

Jane and Bingley’s straightforward mutual attraction serves as a foil to Elizabeth and Darcy’s combative relationship. Their romance appears simple but is disrupted by Darcy and Caroline Bingley, who separate them to protect Bingley from a “disadvantageous” match. Austen shows that even gentle love is vulnerable to class interference.

Key Fact

The Meryton ball introduces every major theme: pride (Darcy’s refusal to dance), prejudice (Elizabeth’s instant judgment), class (the Bennet family’s social embarrassments), and marriage as a public performance. Austen establishes that first impressions in this world are powerful, often wrong, and very difficult to overcome.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When analysing the ball scene, focus on Austen’s use of dialogue to reveal character (AO2). Darcy’s “tolerable” insult and Elizabeth’s witty response establish the dynamic that drives the novel. For AO3, discuss how balls functioned as marriage markets.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Meryton ball establishes the novel’s central dynamic: Darcy judges by class, Elizabeth by character, and both are partially wrong.
  • Darcy’s “tolerable” insult and Elizabeth’s witty response introduce pride and prejudice as mutual flaws.
  • The Bennet family’s social embarrassments show that in Regency England, you were judged by your family, not just yourself.

lessons.title: Wickham, Collins & Darcy's Letter
lessons.description: Wickham’s deception, Collins’s absurd proposal, and Darcy’s rejected declaration at Hunsford.
lessons.content_html:
Wickham’s False Charm

Mr Wickham arrives in Meryton as a handsome, charming militia officer. He quickly befriends Elizabeth and tells her that Darcy cheated him out of a valuable living left to him by Darcy’s father. Elizabeth believes him immediately because his story confirms her existing prejudice against Darcy. Austen shows how prejudice makes us gullible: we trust people who tell us what we already want to believe.

Wickham is a foil to Darcy: charming on the surface but morally bankrupt underneath. Darcy appears proud but is genuinely honourable. Austen’s central irony is that first impressions reverse the truth: the pleasant man is dangerous, the rude man is worthy.

Key Fact

Elizabeth trusts Wickham because his story confirms her existing prejudice against Darcy. Austen shows that prejudice is not just about disliking people — it also means being too ready to trust those who flatter us. Elizabeth’s error mirrors Darcy’s: both judge by first impressions.

Collins’s Proposal and Charlotte’s Choice

Mr Collins proposes to Elizabeth with comic pomposity, listing his “reasons” (Lady Catherine’s approval, his duty as clergyman, the entail) but never mentioning love. Elizabeth refuses firmly, but Collins cannot comprehend her refusal. Austen uses Collins to satirise the transactional nature of Regency marriage — he treats a proposal like a business negotiation.

Charlotte Lucas then accepts Collins, choosing financial security over romantic happiness: “I am not romantic, you know; I never was. I ask only a comfortable home.” Elizabeth is shocked, but Charlotte’s decision is entirely rational within the Regency system. Austen asks the reader to consider whether Elizabeth’s idealism is a luxury only a younger, prettier woman can afford.

Darcy’s first proposal is more insult than declaration. He dwells on Elizabeth’s inferior connections rather than expressing love: “In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.” The word “struggled” and “will not do” frame his love as an affliction. Elizabeth is furious and rejects him passionately: “You are the last man in the world whom I could ever be prevailed on to marry.”

Darcy’s Letter — The Turning Point

Darcy’s letter after the proposal is the novel’s structural turning point. It reveals that Wickham is a liar who attempted to elope with Darcy’s fifteen-year-old sister Georgiana, and that Darcy separated Bingley from Jane to protect his friend from what he considered an unsuitable family. Elizabeth is forced to acknowledge her prejudice: “Till this moment I never knew myself.”

Elizabeth’s epiphany — “Till this moment I never knew myself” — is the novel’s emotional climax. She recognises that her intelligence and wit made her overconfident in her judgments. The letter splits the novel into before (prejudice) and after (self-knowledge). Austen suggests that knowing yourself is harder and more valuable than knowing others.

Key Fact

The letter is the novel’s most important structural device. It provides new information (Wickham’s true character, Georgiana’s near-seduction) while forcing Elizabeth to recognise her own prejudice. Both Darcy and Elizabeth must overcome their flaws — his pride and her prejudice — before they can come together.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For AO2, discuss the epistolary form as a method.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Wickham’s charm conceals dishonesty, while Darcy’s rudeness conceals genuine worth — Austen’s central irony about first impressions.
  • Darcy’s first proposal fails because his pride prevents him from expressing love without class condescension.
  • Elizabeth’s self-recognition after the letter is the novel’s emotional and structural turning point.

lessons.title: Pemberley & Changed Perceptions
lessons.description: The Pemberley visit, Lydia’s elopement with Wickham, and Darcy’s second proposal.
lessons.content_html:
Pemberley — Seeing the Real Darcy

Elizabeth visits Pemberley with her aunt and uncle, the Gardiners. The estate is magnificent but not ostentatious — it reflects taste rather than vulgar display. Darcy’s housekeeper Mrs Reynolds praises him as “the best master” and the kindest man she has ever known. This third-party testimony cannot be dismissed as bias, and it profoundly changes Elizabeth’s view.

When Elizabeth encounters Darcy unexpectedly, he is transformed: warm, attentive and genuinely welcoming to the Gardiners — the very trade connections he previously disdained. Austen shows his transformation through action, not declaration. He proves he has overcome his pride by treating people he would once have snubbed with genuine respect.

Key Fact

Pemberley functions as both setting and symbol. The estate’s beauty and order reflect Darcy’s true character: generous, tasteful and responsible. Elizabeth’s famous thought — “to be mistress of Pemberley might be something!” — is comic, but it also signals her recognition that Darcy’s qualities are real.

Lydia’s Elopement — Scandal and Survival

Lydia’s elopement with Wickham is a catastrophe. In Regency society, an unmarried woman living with a man was ruinous, and one sister’s scandal tainted the whole family’s reputation. All five sisters’ marriage prospects would be destroyed. Mr Bennet’s failure to control Lydia is his greatest parental failure — his detached irony has had real consequences.

Darcy secretly pays Wickham’s debts and arranges the marriage, saving the Bennets from social destruction. He asks for no credit and wants Elizabeth never to know. Austen shows that true love is expressed through selfless action, not grand declarations. The contrast with his insulting first proposal demonstrates genuine transformation.

Darcy’s second proposal is humble and direct: “You are too generous to trifle with me. If your feelings are still what they were last April, tell me so at once.” The language is entirely different from his first attempt — no mention of her inferior connections, no struggle against his feelings. Elizabeth accepts, and both acknowledge their earlier errors. Austen shows that true love requires mutual growth and honest self-knowledge.

Resolution — Four Marriages Compared

The novel’s resolution brings together four contrasting marriages. Charlotte and Collins represent pragmatic survival. Lydia and Wickham represent reckless passion — their marriage is unhappy, held together only by Darcy’s money. Jane and Bingley represent gentle mutual affection. Elizabeth and Darcy represent Austen’s ideal: a union of intellectual equals who have both overcome significant flaws.

Lady Catherine storms to Longbourn to demand that Elizabeth refuse Darcy. Her language reveals pure class snobbery: “Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?” Elizabeth’s refusal to yield — “I am only resolved to act in that manner which will constitute my happiness” — is her finest moment of independence. Ironically, Lady Catherine’s report of Elizabeth’s defiance encourages Darcy to propose again.

Key Fact

Darcy’s transformation is proven through three selfless actions: welcoming the Gardiners at Pemberley, paying Wickham’s debts, and arranging Lydia’s marriage without seeking credit. Austen argues that genuine change shows in behaviour, not in speeches.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions about transformation, contrast Darcy’s first and second proposals directly. Show how specific language changes reflect character growth. For AO3, discuss how Pemberley symbolises the ideal of the responsible landowner.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Pemberley symbolises Darcy’s true character: ordered, beautiful and generous — the opposite of his public manner.
  • Darcy proves his transformation through selfless action (saving the Bennets), not through declarations.
  • The four marriages represent different combinations of love, pragmatism and social pressure in Regency England.

lessons.title: Resolution & Marriage
lessons.description: Lydia’s elopement, Darcy’s intervention, the second proposal, and resolution.
lessons.content_html:
The Lydia Crisis

Lydia’s elopement with Wickham is the novel’s crisis. She runs away from Brighton, believing they will marry. In Regency society, an unmarried woman living with a man was a catastrophic scandal that would ruin her entire family. Mrs Bennet is hysterical. The real question is: who will marry any Bennet sister now that the family name is disgraced?

Wickham has no intention of marrying Lydia — she has no fortune. The elopement exposes his true character as a rake, not the victim he claimed to be. Mr Bennet’s negligence is finally exposed: he retreated into his library while his youngest daughters ran wild. “I am heartily ashamed of myself,” he admits — but the damage is done.

Key Fact

Lydia’s elopement exposes: (1) Wickham’s predatory nature, (2) Mr Bennet’s parental negligence, and (3) the precariousness of women’s reputations in Regency society. One daughter’s scandal threatens all five sisters’ futures.

Darcy’s Secret Intervention

Darcy quietly resolves the crisis. He tracks Wickham and Lydia to London, pays Wickham’s considerable debts, and bribes him to marry Lydia. He does this entirely for Elizabeth’s sake, asking for no recognition. When the Gardiners reveal his role, Elizabeth is astonished: the man she once despised has saved her family at enormous personal cost.

Darcy’s intervention is the novel’s most powerful proof of genuine transformation. He helps the family he once called ‘degrading.’ He pays off the man who tried to seduce his own sister. He asks for nothing in return. This is not pride or obligation — it is selfless love. Austen contrasts Darcy’s actions with Wickham’s: one man sacrifices for love, the other exploits it.

Lady Catherine arrives at Longbourn to demand Elizabeth promise never to accept Darcy. She calls the Bennets “obstinate, headstrong” and asks: “Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?” Elizabeth refuses: “I am only resolved to act in that manner, which will, in my own opinion, constitute my happiness, without reference to you.” This confrontation is Austen’s most direct clash between individual merit and aristocratic entitlement. Elizabeth wins — and Lady Catherine’s report of her defiance ironically encourages Darcy to propose again.

The Second Proposal

Darcy proposes again during a walk near Longbourn. His tone is entirely changed: “an eagerness that had nothing of pride or resentment about it.” He speaks with humility and vulnerability. Elizabeth accepts. Austen deliberately contrasts the two proposals: the first was pride assuming gratitude; the second is genuine love expressed with honest uncertainty.

When Elizabeth tries to explain her changed feelings, she jokes: “I believe I must date it from my first seeing his beautiful grounds at Pemberley.” This is classic Austen — the joke contains truth (Pemberley did influence her) while deflecting from the real, complex process of revised understanding that brought her to this point.

Key Fact

First proposal: pride, ‘degradation,’ expects gratitude, delivered indoors formally. Second proposal: humility, eagerness, no class references, delivered outdoors on a walk. The contrast proves genuine transformation in both characters.

The Resolution

Three marriages conclude the novel (a fourth, Charlotte and Collins, occurred earlier): Elizabeth and Darcy (love with mutual respect), Jane and Bingley (gentle love rewarded), and Lydia and Wickham (a cautionary tale of passion without judgement). Mr Bennet is chastened by the Lydia crisis. Mrs Bennet is delighted — for entirely material reasons: “three daughters married! Ten thousand a year!” Her response confirms that she has learned nothing, providing one final comic irony.

Some critics argue the ending is too neat — the heroine gets the richest man, the villain is punished, the good are rewarded. But Austen includes complications that prevent simple satisfaction. Lydia remains unrepentant. Wickham is bought, not reformed. Mrs Bennet learns nothing. Mr Bennet retreats again. The ideal marriage exists alongside continuing foolishness, suggesting that individual happiness is possible but social reform is not.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When comparing the two proposals, focus on specific language changes. First proposal: ‘degradation,’ ‘against his will.’ Second: ‘eagerness,’ no class references. This precise AO2 comparison, linked to Darcy’s transformation (AO1) and Regency class expectations (AO3), earns top-band marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Lydia’s elopement tests every character and exposes parental failure and social vulnerability.
  • Darcy’s secret intervention — selfless, uncredited, costly — is the ultimate proof of his transformation.
  • The second proposal contrasts perfectly with the first: humility and vulnerability replace pride and condescension.

lessons.title: Character Analysis
lessons.description: Austen’s ironic narrator, free indirect discourse, and how she controls reader sympathies.
lessons.content_html:
Austen’s Ironic Narrative Voice

Austen’s narrative voice operates through irony: the narrator often states the opposite of what she means. The opening sentence presents social prejudice as “universal truth.” This ironic distance runs through every page, shaping how we judge characters without ever directly telling us what to think.

The narrator is often close to Elizabeth’s perspective but is not identical to it. We share Elizabeth’s amusement and anger, but the narrator subtly distances herself when Elizabeth’s judgment fails. This creates dramatic irony — the reader sees what Elizabeth cannot.

Key Fact

Free indirect discourse blends the narrator’s voice with a character’s thoughts, creating dramatic irony. The reader recognises Elizabeth’s errors before she does because the narrator’s ironic distance reveals what the character’s limited perspective cannot.

Free Indirect Discourse

Free indirect discourse is Austen’s signature technique. When we read “Darcy had never been so bewitched by any woman,” we are inside Darcy’s consciousness but hearing the narrator’s words. This blending creates dramatic irony: we simultaneously experience feelings and recognise limitations.

Consider: “Elizabeth, feeling really anxious, was determined to go.” The word “really” feels like Elizabeth’s own thought inserted into the narrator’s sentence. This creates intimacy while maintaining analytical distance.

Consider: “Elizabeth, feeling really anxious, was determined to go to Jane.” The word “really” feels like Elizabeth’s thought inserted into the narrator’s sentence. This blending creates intimacy while maintaining analytical distance. When Elizabeth misjudges Wickham, the narrator’s gentle irony signals the error.

Dialogue as Characterisation

Austen uses dialogue more than description to reveal character. Collins’s proposal exposes his pomposity without narrator commentary. Darcy’s first proposal reveals his pride through his own language. The comedy of manners relies on the gap between social performance and private reality.

Collins lists his “reasons for marrying” without mentioning love. His language is pompous: “Almost as soon as I entered the house, I singled you out.” The word “singled out” makes Elizabeth sound like an item selected from a shelf. Austen needs no narrator commentary — Collins condemns himself.

Key Fact

The opening sentence presents social prejudice as “universal truth.” Collins’s proposal lists “reasons” without love. Darcy’s first proposal insults more than it flatters. Irony is Austen’s primary tool for social critique.

lessons.title: Irony & Narrative Voice
lessons.description: How Austen explores pride, prejudice, class, marriage and reputation across the novel.
lessons.content_html:
Pride and Prejudice — The Central Duality

The title names the novel’s two central flaws. Darcy’s pride makes him dismissive; Elizabeth’s prejudice makes her judge harshly while trusting Wickham’s charm. Both stem from judging by appearance rather than character.

Mary Bennet observes that “vanity and pride are different things”: pride relates to self-opinion, vanity to others’ opinions. Darcy’s pride is eventually compatible with goodness; Mrs Bennet’s vanity is driven by social anxiety.

Key Fact

Mary states “vanity and pride are different things” — pride is justified self-respect, vanity is concern for others’ opinion. Darcy has pride; Mrs Bennet has vanity. The novel asks whether pride can coexist with humility.

Class, Wealth and Social Mobility

Class operates at every level. Lady Catherine represents aristocratic snobbery: “Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?” Caroline Bingley’s contempt reflects new money’s insecurity. Even Elizabeth judges Charlotte’s choice, revealing her own class assumptions about what constitutes an acceptable life.

Austen does not reject the class system entirely — she values taste, education and responsibility. But she argues that these qualities are not the exclusive property of any class. The Gardiners, despite their trade connections, are more refined than many gentlemen.

Lady Catherine demands Elizabeth refuse Darcy: “Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?” The metaphor of “pollution” reveals her view of class as biological purity. Elizabeth’s refusal — “I am only resolved to act in that manner which will constitute my happiness” — is her finest moment.

Marriage and Reputation

Marriage is simultaneously love story and economic transaction. Austen argues the best marriages combine mutual respect, intellectual equality and affection. Reputation is the mechanism through which society controls individuals — Lydia’s scandal shows how one person’s behaviour can destroy an entire family’s prospects.

Pemberley is a physical manifestation of Darcy’s character. The grounds are beautiful but natural, showing taste over ostentation. Elizabeth’s thought — “to be mistress of Pemberley might be something!” — is comic, but Austen also suggests that appreciating Pemberley means appreciating Darcy’s true qualities.

Key Fact

Reputation is social currency. Lydia’s elopement threatens all sisters. Lady Catherine sees Elizabeth as polluting Pemberley’s reputation. Austen shows reputation constrains women more than men — Wickham escapes while Lydia would be destroyed.

lessons.title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
lessons.description: OCR exam technique for Pride and Prejudice: 40-mark responses and quotation skills.
lessons.content_html:
Exam Format Overview

The Pride and Prejudice question will appear on your 19th-century novel paper. It assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3. This is typically a closed-text exam — you will not have the novel in front of you. You may face an extract-based or discursive question. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact format, mark weightings and timing.

Both question types require clear argument, embedded quotations, and woven Assessment Objectives. The examiner rewards responses that analyse Austen’s methods (irony, free indirect discourse, dialogue, symbolism) and embed Regency context within that analysis.

Key Fact

AO1 = ideas and textual references. AO2 = analysis of methods and effects. AO3 = understanding of context. The examiner wants all three woven together, not as separate sections.

Structuring an Analytical Response

Use the WHAT-HOW-WHY model: WHAT (state your point, AO1), HOW (analyse method with quotation, AO2), WHY (embed context, AO3). Begin with a clear thesis and aim for 4–5 analytical paragraphs, adjusting to the time you are given for the question.

Common mistakes: retelling the plot, bolting on context as a separate paragraph, writing about the novel without naming techniques. Every sentence should analyse Austen’s methods and their effects within a sustained argument.

Pride: “tolerable, but not handsome enough” — “My good opinion once lost is lost for ever.” Prejudice: “I could easily forgive his pride” — “Till this moment I never knew myself.” Marriage: “I ask only a comfortable home” — “You are too generous to trifle with me.” Class: “Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?”

Quotation Skills

Memorise short embedded quotations per theme: pride (“tolerable, but not handsome enough”), prejudice (“I could easily forgive his pride”), self-knowledge (“Till this moment I never knew myself”), marriage (“I ask only a comfortable home”), class (“Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?”).

Plot retelling: The examiner knows the story. Bolted-on context: embed it within analysis. Missing AO2: always name techniques (irony, free indirect discourse, dialogue) and explain their effect.

Key Fact

Short embedded quotations are more effective than long passages. Memorise 2–3 per theme and practise weaving them into analytical sentences.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Focus on weaving AO1, AO2 and AO3 together in every analytical paragraph.

options: A summary of the novel's plot in chronological order
Analysis of Austen's methods and their effects on the reader
A list of all the characters and their social positions
Understanding of the historical context of the Regency period only

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is identified as a common mistake students make when writing about Pride and Prejudice?
options: Embedding too many quotations into their own sentences
Analysing Austen's use of irony without naming it
Writing a thesis statement at the start of the essay
Retelling the plot rather than analysing Austen's methods
